title: NORCET — OBG Nursing | Nutrition in Pregnancy
description: Subject-wise test on Nutrition in Pregnancy (OBG Nursing) for NORCET. 30Q.

questions.question: A pregnant woman in her second trimester with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI is advised to increase her daily caloric intake by approximately how many kilocalories to meet increased metabolic demands?

options.explanation: This is too low to meet the increased metabolic demands of pregnancy.
This is lower than the recommended increase for the second trimester.
This is within the recommended range for the second trimester.
This is higher than the recommended increase for the second trimester and more aligned with the third trimester recommendation.

questions.explanation: The recommended increase in daily caloric intake for a pregnant woman with a normal BMI is approximately 340-350 kcal in the second trimester and 450-500 kcal in the third trimester.

questions.question: A primigravida is undergoing antenatal counseling regarding essential micronutrients. The nurse emphasizes the critical role of folic acid supplementation, especially in early pregnancy, primarily to prevent which of the following fetal conditions?

options.explanation: While important, iron deficiency anemia is not the primary condition prevented by folic acid supplementation.
Folic acid supplementation is primarily aimed at preventing neural tube defects.
Gestational diabetes mellitus is not directly prevented by folic acid supplementation.
Preterm birth is not the primary condition targeted by folic acid supplementation.

questions.explanation: Folic acid supplementation, particularly in the periconceptional period and throughout the first trimester, is crucial for preventing neural tube defects (NTDs) such as spina bifida and anencephaly.

questions.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman has a pre-pregnancy Body Mass Index (BMI) of 22 kg/m². What is the recommended total weight gain range for her entire pregnancy?

options.explanation: This range is too low for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI.
This range is also too low for the recommended weight gain for a normal BMI.
This is the recommended weight gain range for women with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI.
This range is slightly higher than the recommended for a normal BMI and is more appropriate for underweight women.

questions.explanation: For women with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI (18.5-24.9 kg/m²), the Institute of Medicine (IOM) recommends a total weight gain during pregnancy of 11.5 to 16 kg (25 to 35 lbs).

questions.question: A pregnant woman is diagnosed with mild iron deficiency anemia. The nurse provides dietary counseling, advising her on food choices that enhance the absorption of non-heme iron. Which of the following food combinations would be most effective for this purpose?

options.explanation: Milk can inhibit iron absorption, making this combination less effective.
The Vitamin C in orange juice enhances the absorption of non-heme iron in lentils.
While red meat is a source of heme iron, tea can inhibit iron absorption, and this combination does not enhance non-heme iron absorption.
Cheese can inhibit iron absorption, and this combination does not effectively enhance non-heme iron absorption.

questions.explanation: Non-heme iron (found in plant-based foods like lentils, spinach) is better absorbed when consumed with Vitamin C (ascorbic acid), which is abundant in orange juice. Milk, tea, and cheese can inhibit iron absorption.

questions.question: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks gestation is admitted to the hospital with severe nausea and vomiting, diagnosed as hyperemesis gravidarum. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial nutritional intervention by the nurse?

options.text: Administering intravenous hyperalimentation immediately to prevent malnutrition.
options.explanation: IV hyperalimentation is typically reserved for more severe cases that do not respond to other interventions.

options.text: Encouraging the intake of large, infrequent meals to reduce gastric emptying.
options.explanation: Large meals can exacerbate nausea and vomiting in hyperemesis gravidarum.

options.text: Offering small, frequent, dry, and bland meals/snacks throughout the day.
options.explanation: This approach minimizes gastric irritation and helps reduce nausea and vomiting.

options.text: Advising consumption of high-fat, fried foods to increase caloric density.
options.explanation: High-fat and fried foods can worsen symptoms of hyperemesis gravidarum.

questions.explanation: For hyperemesis gravidarum, the initial nutritional approach involves offering small, frequent, dry, and bland meals or snacks to minimize gastric irritation and reduce nausea and vomiting. Large meals, high-fat foods, and fried items can exacerbate symptoms. IV hyperalimentation is reserved for severe, refractory cases after other interventions have failed.

questions.question: A pregnant woman who follows a strict vegan diet expresses concern about obtaining all necessary nutrients. Which of the following nutrients is she most likely to be deficient in, requiring careful dietary planning or supplementation?

options.explanation: Vitamin C is abundant in many fruits and vegetables, making deficiency less common in vegans who consume a variety of these foods.
Folic acid is found in leafy greens and legumes, making it less likely to be deficient in a well-planned vegan diet.
Vitamin B12 is primarily found in animal products, making it difficult for vegans to obtain sufficient amounts without supplementation or fortified foods.
While iron deficiency can be a concern in vegan diets, it is not as exclusively linked to veganism as Vitamin B12 deficiency.

questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is primarily found in animal products. Individuals following a strict vegan diet are at high risk for Vitamin B12 deficiency and typically require fortified foods or supplementation. While iron can also be a concern, B12 deficiency is almost exclusively linked to vegan diets without supplementation.

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman is 160 cm tall and weighs 45 kg at her first antenatal visit in the first trimester. Based on her pre-pregnancy status, what is her calculated BMI, and what is the recommended total weight gain range for her entire pregnancy?

options.explanation: The recommended weight gain range for a BMI of 17.6 kg/m² is not 11.5-16 kg, as this range is for women with a normal BMI.
The calculated BMI is 17.6 kg/m², which falls into the underweight category, and the recommended weight gain for underweight women is 12.5 to 18 kg.
The calculated BMI is not 19.5 kg/m², and the recommended weight gain range for a normal BMI is not 7-11.5 kg.
The calculated BMI is not 19.5 kg/m², which would correspond to a normal weight category, and the recommended gain for this BMI category is not applicable here.

questions.explanation: 1. Calculate BMI: Height in meters = 160 cm / 100 = 1.6 m, BMI = Weight (kg) / (Height (m))^2, BMI = 45 kg / (1.6 m)^2 = 45 kg / 2.56 m² = 17.578 kg/m² ≈ 17.6 kg/m². 2. Determine BMI Category: A BMI of 17.6 kg/m² falls into the underweight category (BMI < 18.5 kg/m²). 3. Recommended Weight Gain: For underweight women, the recommended total weight gain during pregnancy is 12.5 to 18 kg (28 to 40 lbs).

questions.question: A 30-year-old primigravida is diagnosed with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) at 28 weeks gestation. She expresses anxiety about managing her blood sugar through diet. Which of the following dietary strategies is the most appropriate for the nurse to recommend?

options.text: Eliminating all carbohydrate-containing foods to maintain tight glycemic control.
options.explanation: Eliminating all carbohydrate-containing foods is not a balanced or sustainable approach to managing blood sugar levels.

options.text: Consuming large amounts of fruit juice and sweetened beverages
options.explanation: Consuming large amounts of fruit juice and sweetened beverages would likely exacerbate hyperglycemia and is not a recommended dietary strategy for managing GDM.

options.text: Following a balanced meal plan that includes protein, healthy fats, and complex carbohydrates
options.explanation: A balanced meal plan that includes protein, healthy fats, and complex carbohydrates can help regulate blood sugar levels and provide essential nutrients for the patient and her fetus.

options.text: Drastically reducing calorie intake to promote weight loss
options.explanation: Drastically reducing calorie intake is not a recommended approach to managing GDM, as it can lead to nutrient deficiencies and other complications.

questions.explanation: The nurse should recommend a balanced diet that takes into account the patient's individual needs and health status.

questions.question: A pregnant woman with a normal pre-pregnancy Body Mass Index (BMI) asks the nurse about the recommended daily caloric increase during the second trimester. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.explanation: This is not the recommended daily caloric increase for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI during the second trimester.
This is the recommended daily caloric increase for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI during the second trimester.
This is the recommended daily caloric increase for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI during the third trimester, not the second trimester.

options.text: No additional caloric intake is necessary if she eats a balanced diet
options.explanation: This is not accurate, as a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI does require additional caloric intake during the second and third trimesters.

questions.explanation: For a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI, the recommended daily caloric increase is approximately 340 kcal/day during the second trimester and 450-500 kcal/day during the third trimester. The first trimester generally requires no significant additional caloric intake.

questions.question: A G1P0 client at 8 weeks gestation is concerned about preventing neural tube defects. Which of the following nutrients should the nurse emphasize as crucial during early pregnancy for this purpose?

options.explanation: While iron is important during pregnancy, it is not the primary nutrient for preventing neural tube defects.
While calcium is important for fetal bone development, it is not the primary nutrient for preventing neural tube defects.
Folic acid is the primary nutrient for preventing neural tube defects during early pregnancy.
While Vitamin D is important for bone health, it is not the primary nutrient for preventing neural tube defects.

questions.explanation: Folic acid (Vitamin B9) is critically important in the periconceptional period (before and during early pregnancy) to prevent neural tube defects such as spina bifida and anencephaly.

questions.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester has a hemoglobin level of 9.8 g/dL. The nurse is providing education on iron supplementation. Which instruction is most appropriate for maximizing iron absorption?

options.text: Take the iron supplement with milk to prevent stomach upset.
options.explanation: Milk contains calcium, which can inhibit iron absorption.

options.text: Take the iron supplement immediately before bedtime.
options.explanation: Taking iron before bedtime may cause gastrointestinal upset for some individuals.

options.text: Take the iron supplement with a glass of orange juice.
options.explanation: Vitamin C in orange juice enhances iron absorption.

options.text: Take the iron supplement on an empty stomach with coffee.
options.explanation: Coffee contains tannins, which can inhibit iron absorption.

questions.explanation: Iron absorption is enhanced by Vitamin C (ascorbic acid), which is found in orange juice. Taking iron with milk (calcium inhibits absorption) or coffee/tea (tannins inhibit absorption) should be avoided. Taking it before bedtime might cause gastrointestinal upset for some, and while an empty stomach is generally recommended, combining it with Vitamin C is key for absorption.

questions.question: A pregnant client, 16 weeks gestation, reports experiencing 'pica' and has been craving and consuming significant amounts of clay. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.text: Advise the client that pica is a normal pregnancy craving and will resolve postpartum.
options.explanation: Pica is not a normal pregnancy craving and can indicate underlying nutritional deficiencies.

options.text: Recommend increasing fiber intake to manage potential constipation from clay consumption.
options.explanation: While fiber intake is important, it does not address the underlying cause of pica.

options.text: Counsel the client to switch from clay to ice chips, as ice is less harmful.
options.explanation: Switching to ice chips does not address the underlying nutritional deficiencies causing pica.

options.text: Assess for potential underlying nutritional deficiencies, particularly iron-deficiency anemia.
options.explanation: Assessing for nutritional deficiencies, especially iron-deficiency anemia, is crucial when a client reports pica.

questions.explanation: Pica, the craving and consumption of non-nutritive substances, is often associated with iron-deficiency anemia in pregnancy. The priority is to assess and address any underlying nutritional deficiencies, as consuming non-food items can lead to adverse health effects for both mother and fetus.

questions.question: Which of the following dietary recommendations is most appropriate for a pregnant woman to ensure adequate protein intake?

options.text: Consume at least 2 servings of fruits and vegetables daily.
options.explanation: While fruits and vegetables are important, they are not the primary sources of protein.

options.text: Limit intake of all dairy products to reduce fat consumption.
options.explanation: Dairy products are a good source of protein, and limiting them may not be necessary for all pregnant women.

options.text: Include lean meats, poultry, fish, eggs, and legumes in daily meals.
options.explanation: These foods are excellent sources of protein and should be included in daily meals to ensure adequate protein intake.

options.text: Prioritize complex carbohydrates such as whole grains for energy.
options.explanation: While complex carbohydrates are important for energy, they are not the primary source of protein.

questions.explanation: Protein is essential for fetal growth and development, as well as maternal tissue expansion. Lean meats, poultry, fish, eggs, and legumes are excellent sources of protein.

questions.question: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks gestation is diagnosed with gestational diabetes. Which nutritional counseling point is most crucial for her to manage her blood glucose levels effectively?

options.text: Completely eliminate all carbohydrates from her diet.
options.explanation: Completely eliminating carbohydrates is not necessary or recommended for gestational diabetes management.

options.text: Consume large, infrequent meals to prevent hunger.
options.explanation: Large, infrequent meals can cause spikes in blood glucose levels and are not recommended for gestational diabetes management.

options.text: Distribute carbohydrate intake evenly throughout the day in small, frequent meals.
options.explanation: This approach helps to prevent large spikes in blood glucose levels and is recommended for gestational diabetes management.

options.text: Focus solely on high-protein, high-fat foods.
options.explanation: While protein and fat are important, focusing solely on these macronutrients is not recommended for gestational diabetes management.

questions.explanation: For gestational diabetes, the most crucial nutritional advice is to distribute carbohydrate intake evenly throughout the day in smaller, more frequent meals. This helps to prevent large spikes in blood glucose levels that can occur with large, infrequent meals or excessive carbohydrate intake at one time.

questions.question: A 25-year-old primigravida, who is a strict vegan, is at 10 weeks gestation. She expresses concern about meeting all her nutritional needs. Which two micronutrients are of particular concern for this client, and what advice should the nurse provide?

options.text: Calcium and Vitamin C; Advise increased intake of citrus fruits and fortified cereals.
options.explanation: While calcium and Vitamin C are important, they are not the primary micronutrients of concern for a vegan pregnant woman.

options.text: Iron and Vitamin A; Advise consuming more leafy greens and carrots.
options.explanation: While iron is a concern, Vitamin A is not the primary micronutrient of concern for a vegan pregnant woman.

options.text: Vitamin B12 and Iron; Advise fortified foods, B12 supplements, and iron-rich plant foods with Vitamin C.
options.explanation: Vitamin B12 and iron are the primary micronutrients of concern for a vegan pregnant woman, and the nurse should advise on fortified foods, supplements, and iron-rich plant foods with Vitamin C.

options.text: Folate and Zinc; Advise consuming more legumes and whole grains.
options.explanation: While folate and zinc are important, they are not the primary micronutrients of concern for a vegan pregnant woman.

questions.explanation: Strict vegan diets often lack sufficient Vitamin B12 (found almost exclusively in animal products) and readily absorbable iron (heme iron from animal sources). The nurse should advise fortified foods (e.g., plant milks, nutritional yeast for B12), a Vitamin B12 supplement, and consuming non-heme iron sources (legumes, dark leafy greens) along with Vitamin C-rich foods to enhance absorption.

questions.question: A pregnant client living in a region with known iodine deficiency reports consuming only non-iodized salt and rarely eats seafood. What potential fetal complication should the nurse be most concerned about due to this dietary habit?

options.explanation: Neural tube defects are primarily associated with folic acid deficiency, not iodine deficiency.
Macrosomia is not directly related to iodine deficiency.
Iodine deficiency can lead to congenital hypothyroidism and impaired neurodevelopment in the fetus.
Iron-deficiency anemia is not directly related to iodine deficiency.

questions.explanation: Iodine is essential for the production of thyroid hormones, which play a critical role in fetal brain development. Severe iodine deficiency during pregnancy can lead to congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism) and irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment in the child.

questions.question: A G2P1 client at 32 weeks gestation presents for a routine check-up. She has a history of gestational hypertension in her previous pregnancy and is now concerned about her diet. She asks about specific foods to avoid to prevent preeclampsia. Which of the following statements by the nurse reflects the most current evidence-based understanding regarding diet and preeclampsia prevention?

options.text: Strictly limit your sodium intake to prevent fluid retention and high blood pressure.
options.explanation: Strict sodium restriction is not recommended for preeclampsia prevention.

options.text: Focus on a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet to reduce your risk.
options.explanation: There is no evidence to support a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet for preeclampsia prevention.

options.text: While no specific diet can guarantee prevention, ensure adequate calcium and Vitamin D, and aim for a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains.
options.explanation: This statement reflects the most current evidence-based understanding regarding diet and preeclampsia prevention.

options.text: Avoid all saturated fats and cholesterol, as these are directly linked to preeclampsia development.
options.explanation: There is no direct link between saturated fats, cholesterol, and preeclampsia development.

questions.explanation: Current evidence does not support specific dietary interventions (like strict sodium restriction or high-protein diets) as definitive preventive measures for preeclampsia. While a healthy, balanced diet is always recommended, the most evidence-based nutritional advice for preeclampsia prevention often includes ensuring adequate calcium and Vitamin D, particularly in at-risk populations.
